title: 2D Shapes and 3D Objects: Names, Attributes and Position
seo_title: Kindergarten 2D shapes and 3D objects Worksheets: Free Math with Pictures and Answers (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Single attributes of 2D shapes and 3D objects: sorting 2D shapes and 3D objects using a single attribute, building and describing 3D objects, exploring, creating, and describing 2D shapes, using positional language, such as beside, on top of, under, and in front of
meta_desc: Free Kindergarten math worksheets on 2D shapes and 3D objects for the BC curriculum: name shapes, sides and corners, spheres, cubes, cylinders and cones, sorting by one attribute, and position words. 100 picture questions with answers.
key_big: 2D shapes are flat; 3D objects are solid.
key_sub: Count straight sides and corners. Some 3D objects roll, some stack, some slide.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • 2D shapes are flat: circle, triangle, square, rectangle. Count the straight sides and the corners.
  • A shape keeps its name when it is turned or a different colour or size.
  • 3D objects are solid: sphere, cube, cylinder, cone. Some roll, some stack, some slide.
  • Position words tell where something is: above, under, beside, in front of, behind.

Examples

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do
Thinking a turned square is not a squareCount the sides and corners. It still has 4 equal sides.
Counting a curved edge as a sideSides are straight. A circle has no straight sides.
Mixing up in front of and behindIn front of is closer to you. Behind is hidden by the other thing.

faq.q: What shapes do Kindergarten children learn in BC?
faq.a: Flat 2D shapes such as circles, triangles, squares and rectangles, and solid 3D objects such as spheres, cubes, cylinders and cones.
One feature, such as the number of sides, the colour, or whether an object rolls. Children sort shapes using one attribute at a time.

faq.q: What is the difference between 2D and 3D?
faq.a: 2D shapes are flat, like a drawing. 3D objects are solid and can be picked up, like a ball or a box.
Words like above, under, beside, in front of and behind help children describe where things are, which is the start of geometry and maps.
